fact_sheet.business_description: Delta operates a global airline network that includes premium cabin services, corporate travel relationships, and a loyalty business [D01]. The company also maintains a refinery, which influences the calculation of GAAP revenue versus adjusted airline revenue [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Passenger air travel services sold to individual and corporate customers, characterized as a repeat-purchase service [D01].
Premium and loyalty program offerings, with American Express remuneration growing 12% to $2 billion in the September quarter [D01].
economics: Business requires significant ongoing investment in aircraft, engines, maintenance, labor, and airport operations [D01].
September quarter adjusted revenue was $15.2 billion with pre-tax income of approximately $1.5 billion [D01].
September quarter gross capital spending was approximately $1.1 billion [D01].
earnings_record: September quarter GAAP diluted EPS was $2.17; adjusted EPS was $1.71 [D01].
Full-year 2025 adjusted EPS guidance was approximately $6 [D01].
competitive_position: Network airline peers include United and American; Southwest is noted as a different operating model [D06].
Management asserts differentiation through premium and loyalty revenue, though the release notes these results were aided by lapping the previous year's CrowdStrike-caused outage [D01, D03].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Debt and finance-lease obligations were $14.9 billion [D01].
Liquidity of $6.9 billion includes $3.1 billion in undrawn revolvers [D01].
management_and_capital_allocation: Ed Bastian is CEO (referenced via issuer claims) [D01].
Management provided full-year free cash flow guidance of $3.5-$4.0 billion [D01].
price_and_valuation: Valuation is approximately 11.57 times management's indicated $6 adjusted annual EPS guidance [D04].

yields_pct.basis: No standardized trailing or owner earnings yield provided in pack; full-year adjusted EPS guidance used for P/E [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Risk of recession, fuel-price shocks, or operational disruptions impacting margins [D05].

final.memo:
We have reviewed Delta Air Lines and determined it does not meet our standards for inclusion in the Berkshire Hathaway portfolio [D01, D08]. The airline industry is fundamentally a capital-intensive commodity business characterized by high operating leverage and the need for constant, massive reinvestment in aircraft and infrastructure [D01, D05].

Our experience has shown that this industry is prone to cyclicality and external shocks that make consistent, long-term earnings records difficult to achieve [D01, D05]. The company currently carries $14.9 billion in debt and finance-lease obligations, which poses a significant risk to the durability of the business during periods of economic contraction [D01].

While the market may focus on adjusted earnings guidance of $6.00 per share, this does not compensate for the inherent risks and capital demands of the sector [D01, D04]. Investing in airlines is akin to buying a ticket to a perpetual race where the participants must constantly spend their winnings just to stay on the track.

We have no current position in the sector and continue to believe that our capital is better allocated to businesses with durable competitive advantages and lower capital requirements [D08]. We prefer to sit on our cash rather than risk a permanent loss of capital in businesses we cannot confidently project for the coming decades [D05, D08].
